description: The Union Budget is the Annual Financial Statement of the Government of India. It provides a comprehensive breakdown of estimated receipts and expenditures for the upcoming financial year, making it a highly crucial topic for competitive exams.

sections.title: Constitutional Provisions
sections.description: Major articles in the Indian Constitution related to the Budget and financial management.

polity_articles.details: The term 'Budget' is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution; instead, it is referred to as the 'Annual Financial Statement'.
Deals with matters related to taxation, public borrowing, and the withdrawal of funds from the Consolidated Fund.
No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India by the government without the constitutional passage of this bill.
All revenues received, loans raised, and money received in repayment of loans by the government are credited to this fund.

sections.title: Key Concepts of the Budget
sections.description: Important economic and financial terminologies frequently used in budget documents.

key_concepts.explanation: The difference between Total Revenue Expenditure and Total Revenue Receipts. It indicates that the government cannot meet its regular, day-to-day expenses from its regular income.
The difference between Total Expenditure and Total Receipts (excluding borrowings). It accurately represents the total borrowing requirements of the government.
Calculated by deducting Interest Payments on previous loans from the Fiscal Deficit. It reflects the true measure of the current financial status of the government.
Government spending that creates physical or financial assets (such as infrastructure, hospitals, and schools) or reduces overall liabilities.

sections.title: Key Themes of Recent Budget: Viksit Bharat
sections.description: The main priorities of the recent budget aimed at transforming India into a developed nation by 2047.

key_concepts.explanation: The government's comprehensive vision and roadmap to transform India into a developed economy by the 100th year of its Independence.
The four main focus areas of the government: G - Garib (Poor), Y - Yuva (Youth), A - Annadata (Farmer), and N - Nari (Women). Their progress is viewed as the country's progress.

important_facts.fact: In the recent budget, the Fiscal Deficit target was set at 4.9% of the GDP, with a strategic aim to bring it below 4.5% in the coming years.
To boost infrastructure development, the Capital Expenditure (CapEx) outlay was significantly increased to 3.4% of the GDP.

sections.title: Major Schemes and Allocations
sections.description: Crucial government schemes announced or highlighted in the budget and their targeted beneficiaries.

key_associations.item: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana
key_associations.extra_info: Aims to provide up to 300 units of free electricity every month to 1 crore households across the country.
A scheme designed to financially empower rural women, with its target recently increased to cover 3 crore women.
The collateral-free loan limit under the 'Tarun' category has been enhanced from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 20 lakh.
A highly successful scheme providing affordable micro-credit facilities to urban street vendors.

sections.title: Historical Budget Facts
sections.description: Important trivia and milestones from the history of the Indian Budget, frequently asked in Static GK.

historical_events.significance: The very first budget of India was introduced during British rule by Scottish economist James Wilson.
Presented by India's first Finance Minister, R. K. Shanmukham Chetty.
Presented by John Mathai. This specific budget laid out the roadmap for the formation of the Planning Commission.
Ending a 92-year-old British-era practice, the Railway Budget was officially merged into the General Budget.

important_facts.fact: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman broke Morarji Desai's record by presenting 7 consecutive Union Budgets.
Morarji Desai holds the overall record for presenting the maximum number of budgets (10 times) in the history of Independent India.
The longest budget speech in Indian history was delivered by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in 2020, lasting 2 hours and 42 minutes.
